name: Mongol Empire
region: Central & East Asia, Middle East, Eastern Europe
summary: The largest contiguous land empire in history, founded by Genghis Khan. It split into four khanates after 1260.

knownFor.label: Yam relay post
knownFor.note: A network of horse relay stations.

location.value: From Mongolia it expanded to cover China, Central Asia, Iran, Iraq, the Caucasus and Russia: the largest contiguous land empire in history.

terrain.value: The Mongolian steppe (grasslands suited to horses), deserts (Gobi), and then the settled lands of China, Persia and Russia.

climate.value: Harsh continental steppe climate. Some researchers link a run of unusually wet, mild years around 1211–1225 to more grass and horses for Genghis Khan’s expansion.

resources.value: Horses and livestock, plus the wealth, artisans and taxes of conquered settled societies.

disasters.value: The Black Death, which spread along Mongol-controlled routes in the 1340s.

population.value: Not stated in Wikipedia. The Mongols themselves numbered perhaps around one million, ruling over a hundred million or more subjects. Conquests caused very large population losses in China, Iran and elsewhere.

urbanisation.value: Capitals at Avarga (1206–1235) and Karakorum (1235–1271), then Khanbaliq (Beijing) under the Yuan.

disease.value: The Black Death spread across Eurasia in the 1340s, partly along trade routes the Mongols connected.

migration.value: Moved artisans, soldiers and administrators across Eurasia, e.g. Persian engineers to China and Chinese experts to Persia.

economicBase.value: Pastoral nomadism, plus tribute and taxes from conquered settled peoples, and trade.

tradeRoutes.value: The “Pax Mongolica” made the Silk Road safer, encouraging trade and travellers such as Marco Polo.

moneyAndTax.value: Various currencies: silver coins, paper money backed by silver (sukhe), and in the Yuan the jiaochao paper currency.

inequality.value: Genghis’ family (the “Golden Lineage”) and Mongol nobles at the top, then allied peoples, then conquered subjects.

governmentType.value: An elective monarchy (later also hereditary) under a Great Khan (khagan), chosen at an assembly (kurultai) of princes.

keyRulers.value: Genghis Khan (1206–1227). Ögedei (1229–1241). Güyük (1246–1248). Möngke (1251–1259). Kublai Khan (1260–1294, nominal Great Khan).

succession.value: Decided by kurultai assemblies, often after long disputes between branches of Genghis’ family. The succession fight after Möngke split the empire.

institutions.value: The Yassa law code, a decimal army organisation (units of 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000), a census, and the yam relay postal system.

stability.value: The Toluid Civil War between Kublai and Ariq Böke (1260–1264), after which the empire divided into four khanates.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the lines of Genghis’ sons (Ögedei, Chagatai, Jochi and Tolui). The Toluids won control of the Great Khanate.

armyAndTech.value: Mounted archers with composite bows, extreme mobility and discipline. Probably only 50,000–75,000 soldiers under Genghis Khan. Adopted Chinese and Muslim siege engineers and gunpowder weapons.

majorWars.value: Conquest of the Jin (to 1234). The destruction of Khwarezm (1219–1221). The invasion of Europe (Mohi, 1241). The sack of Baghdad (1258). Defeat at Ain Jalut (1260). Conquest of Song China (to 1279). Failed invasions of Japan (1274, 1281).

territoryChange.value: About 4.0 million km² (1206), 13.5 million (1227) and 23.5 million (1294), per the Wikipedia infobox.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Jin and Song, Khwarezm, the Abbasids, the Mamluks of Egypt, Japan and Đại Việt. Some European and Armenian rulers sought alliances against the Mamluks.

inventions.value: Spread technologies rather than inventing them: gunpowder, printing, paper money and siege engines moved across Eurasia.

scienceEducation.value: Adopted the Uyghur script for Mongolian. Supported Persian observatories (Maragheh) and exchange between Chinese and Islamic science.

openness.value: Very open to foreign skills and religions, recruiting experts and officials from every conquered people.

communicationTransport.value: The yam relay system: horse stations about every 30–50 km let messengers ride up to about 200 km a day; paiza passes for official travellers.

religion.value: Tengrism (sky worship) and shamanism at first, with tolerance of all religions. Later khanates converted: the Ilkhanate to Islam (Ghazan, 1295), the Yuan court to Tibetan Buddhism.

languageWriting.value: Middle Mongol written in the Uyghur script, plus Turkic languages, Chinese and Persian.

artsArchitecture.value: The Secret History of the Mongols. Patronage of Persian miniature painting and historical writing (Rashid al-Din). Yuan drama and porcelain.

socialStructure.value: Genghis’ family, nobles, warriors, herders, and conquered artisans and peoples, sometimes enslaved or moved as skilled labour.

sharedIdentity.value: Genghis Khan reorganised the steppe tribes into a single “Great Mongol Nation” (Yeke Mongghol Ulus).

dailyLife.value: Round felt gers (yurts) that moved with the herds; meat, milk, cheese and airag (fermented mare’s milk).

neighbours.value: China (Jin, Song), Korea, Central Asian states, Khwarezm, the Abbasids, Rus’ principalities, Hungary, Poland and the Mamluks.

ideasReligions.value: Connected Europe and Asia: Marco Polo, missionaries and merchants travelled freely. Knowledge, crops, technology, and also disease, moved across Eurasia.

colonisation.value: A conquering empire whose campaigns caused great destruction (e.g. in Khwarezm and Baghdad), then ruled conquered peoples through local officials.

riseSignals.value: Genghis Khan united the steppe tribes (1206), built a disciplined army based on loyalty rather than tribe, and adopted the skills of conquered peoples.

peakPeriod.value: The mid-13th century, under Ögedei and Möngke. Greatest extent by 1294 (about 23.5 million km²).

declineSignals.value: Succession disputes, the 1260–64 civil war, division into four rival khanates, defeat at Ain Jalut (1260), and later plague and rebellion.

outcome.value: Fragmentation into successor states: the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan dynasty. The Yuan lost China in 1368.

sources.value: The Secret History of the Mongols, Persian histories (Juvaini, Rashid al-Din), Chinese records, and European travellers (Carpini, Rubruck, Marco Polo). Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Morgan (2007).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Area figures are well established, but population losses, army sizes and destruction are debated, as many sources were written by victims or enemies. Karakorum’s use as capital is dated to 1260 or 1271.
